sentences.text: The storm hit around eight-thirty.
It came all at once.
The wind that had been howling became a scream.
The rain that had been falling became a solid wall of water hitting the cabin.
The tin roof made a sound Aiko had never heard before — a continuous drumming that was almost like a machine.
The walls of the cabin shook.
She could feel them shake.
She was sitting on the floor beside the fire, wrapped in a blanket, and every so often the whole cabin creaked in a way that sounded like it was going to break apart.
Kai sat beside her.
He did not do very much.
He just sat there.
Sometimes he put another log on the fire.
Sometimes he checked the window boards.
Once he got up and checked the radio and reported to the coast guard that they were fine — his voice, on the radio, was clear and calm.
The coast guard said the storm was at its peak, and would begin to drop in about two hours.
Kai came back and sat down beside Aiko.
She leaned against his shoulder.
He put his arm around her.
Neither of them said anything.
There was too much noise to talk anyway.
The worst was around ten p.m.
There was a very big gust of wind, and something outside made a huge cracking noise — a tree, maybe, or a section of fence — and then a heavy thud against the western wall of the cabin.
Aiko jumped.
Kai did not.
He said, "It is okay.
Something hit the wall.
But the wall is not broken.
Listen.
Nothing is coming in." Aiko listened.
Nothing was coming in.
The wall was holding.
She let out a breath.
"I hate this," she said.
Kai laughed a small laugh.
He said, "I hate it too.
I have hated this every storm we have ever had.
Do not think this is easy for me.
I am scared.
I have always been scared.
But being scared and knowing what to do can happen at the same time.
That is what Dad says.
That is what he taught me.
You can be really scared and you can still do the right thing.
In fact, if you are scared, that means you know things.
If you were not scared, that would mean you did not understand what was happening." Aiko thought about this.
She thought — that is a good thing to know.
The storm went on all night.
Around two in the morning it started to drop a little.
Around four it dropped a lot.
By five it was just heavy rain.
By six it was just rain.
By seven the sun was coming up somewhere behind the clouds, and the rain was letting up, and the cabin was still standing.
Aiko had fallen asleep sometime after midnight, curled up on the floor with her head in Kai's lap.
Kai had stayed awake the whole time.
He had put logs on the fire every hour.
He had watched the window.
He had listened to the walls.
He had not slept.
When Aiko woke up it was full daylight.
The storm was gone.
Kai was still sitting where he had been.
His eyes were red and he looked exhausted.
She sat up.
She said, "Did you sleep at all." "No," said Kai.
"Are you tired." "Very," said Kai.
"Okay," said Aiko.
"Go to sleep.
I am going to keep watch now.
You can sleep.
I have got it." Kai looked at her.
He laughed a small tired laugh.
He said, "There is nothing to keep watch for anymore, Aiko.
The storm is over." "I know," said Aiko.
"But I want to keep watch.
Go to sleep." And Kai — because he was exhausted and because he trusted her — lay down beside the fire, and he closed his eyes, and within a minute he was asleep.
Aiko sat beside him.
She kept watch.
Their parents came back on the afternoon ferry the next day, and the water taxi brought them out to the cabin.
Their mother was crying before she was even out of the boat.
Their father — who looked, Aiko thought, a little more tired than he had two days ago — was not crying, but his eyes were bright.
He hugged both of them at once.
He said, into their hair, "You are okay.
You are both okay.
Thank god.
Thank god."
That evening at supper, their father asked Kai what had happened.
Kai told him.
He told him everything he had done.
He told him about the storm procedure.
He told him about the tree that had hit the cabin.
He told him about the radio calls.
He was completely factual.
He did not brag.
He did not make himself sound heroic.
He just reported.
Their father listened.
Their father did not say anything at the end.
He only looked at Kai for a long moment.
Then he put his hand on Kai's shoulder.
He said, "You did well, son.
You did — you did everything I would have done.
You did more than that.
You kept your sister calm.
That is the hardest part.
Thank you."
After that night, Aiko saw her brother differently.
She did not tell him.
She did not have to.
She just — knew.
She knew he was not the person she had thought he was.
She had been wrong.
Not in a way she had to apologize for; Kai had told her he had made himself look that way on purpose.
But she knew, now, that when there was a real problem, Kai was the person she wanted to be next to.
She knew he was going to be someone she looked to for the rest of her life.
Their father did have the heart surgery.
He was on the mainland for six weeks.
Their mother went with him.
Aiko and Kai stayed at the cabin.
Sometimes the Kimura family checked in on them.
But mostly it was just the two of them.
Kai cooked most of the meals.
Aiko did most of the tidying.
They had a rhythm together that had not existed before that one storm night.
When their father came back, healthy again, and things went back to something like normal, Aiko still went and sat on Kai's floor sometimes, when he was reading.
She would just be there for a while.
Kai would not say much.
He never did.
But he would look up from his book, and he would smile at her, and she would smile back, and that was enough.
